common_name: James Walker Bougainvillea (Vigorous Bicolor Orange-to-Magenta Tropical Vine)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; James Walker is an old, widely grown, especially vigorous cultivar suited to large trellises, arbors, and fence lines.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun and provide sturdy support, since James Walker is an unusually strong, fast-growing selection capable of scaling a two-story trellis or arbor in a few seasons. The bracts emerge a warm orange before maturing to a rich reddish-magenta, giving mature plants a striking bicolor effect across a single flush of bloom. Like other bougainvillea, it flowers most heavily when kept on the lean side for water and nitrogen, and hard pruning after major bloom flushes encourages denser rebloom rather than rangy growth. Protect from hard freezes in zone 9, where plants are usually grown against a warm south-facing wall or cut back and allowed to resprout from the base after a mild winter.

common_name: Texas Dawn Bougainvillea (Bougainvillea 'Monas', Vigorous Rose-Pink Clustered-Bloom Vine)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Texas Dawn (cultivar name Monas) was selected for reliable performance and rebloom in hot, humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and tie or weave long canes onto a trellis, arbor, or wall, since Texas Dawn produces long, arching branches rather than a compact form. The comparatively small rose-pink bracts are borne in dense, huge clusters that give the whole plant a solid wash of color from late spring through fall, and the cultivar is noted for continuing to flush new bloom after being cut back hard. It performs reliably through Gulf Coast heat and humidity and tolerates poor, sandy soils once established, but resents standing water and should be kept on the dry side between waterings. In zone 9, site against a warm wall for winter protection or expect dieback to the crown after hard freezes, with recovery from the roots in spring.

common_name: Vera Deep Purple Bougainvillea (Compact Thornless Dwarf Patio Bougainvillea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Vera Deep Purple is a compact, nearly thornless patented cultivar bred for pots, borders, and small spaces rather than large-scale climbing.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Vera Deep Purple stays naturally bushy and upright without the sprawling habit of vining bougainvillea, making it well suited to patio containers, mixed borders, and small courtyard gardens. The deep reddish-purple bracts surround small cream-white true flowers and are produced in heavy flushes from spring through fall, with the nearly thornless stems making the plant easier to handle when deadheading spent bracts or repotting. As with all bougainvillea, restrict water and fertilizer once established to encourage heavier bloom over leafy growth, and bring potted plants under cover before frost outside of zone 10-11. Its compact size also makes it a good candidate for standard (tree-form) training.

common_name: Aloha Red Mandevilla (Vigorous Climbing Mandevilla with Large Bright Red Flowers)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9 plant March-May. Aloha Red is an Australian-bred selection from the Aloha mandevilla series that grows as a true climber when given support.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide a trellis, obelisk, or fence for the twining stems to climb, since Aloha Red is more vine-like and vigorous than compact patio dipladenia types. Large, glossy-throated, bright red trumpet flowers open continuously from late spring through fall against dark green foliage, and deadheading is unnecessary as spent blooms drop cleanly. If left without support the plant will mound and flower densely from the ground up, making it flexible for both trellis and large container use. In zone 9, grow in a protected, warm microclimate or bring containers indoors before the first frost, since the plant is killed by freezing temperatures; wear gloves when pruning, as the milky sap can irritate skin.

common_name: Diamantina Coral Orange Sunrise Dipladenia (Compact Coral-Orange Mandevilla with Yellow Throat)
scientific_name: Mandevilla x hybrida 'Diamantina Coral Orange Sunrise'

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9 plant March-May. Diamantina Coral Orange Sunrise is a compact, early-flowering dipladenia-type mandevilla bred for containers and hanging baskets.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic potting mix; Diamantina Coral Orange Sunrise forms a dense, mounding, self-branching plant rather than a long climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and performs best in patio containers, hanging baskets, and window boxes. The coral-to-orange trumpet flowers with yellow throats open earlier in the season and more heavily than older mandevilla types, covering the compact plant in continuous color from spring through fall. Regular light feeding through the growing season sustains the heavy bloom count, and the plant tolerates brief dry spells well once established, though consistent moisture during peak summer heat keeps flowering steady. Outside of zone 10-11, grow as a warm-season container annual or overwinter indoors in bright light, since it has no cold tolerance; wear gloves when handling cut stems, as the sap can irritate skin.
